And the problem is, I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. I’ll be right in the middle of a batch of files—and we have these quotas we're supposed to hit, so I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish my claim reviews—but I just find myself walking away from my desk. I'll get up to go to the breakroom to fill my water bottle even if it's already full, or I'll just walk down the hall, or I'll go over to someone else's cubicle to ask a question that definitely could have just been an instant message. 

It’s like, I know I need to stay in my chair, the work is right there on my screen, and I tell myself, "Okay, just sit here until this stack is done," but I just... I can't seem to stay glued to the seat. I just keep leaving my desk, and it's really starting to become a noticeable issue with my productivity. My supervisor hasn't formally written me up yet, but I can tell she's noticing that I'm never at my desk when she walks by, so I figured I really needed to talk to a doctor about it before it turns into a bigger deal.

If I see a file in there that I know is going to need a really long written explanation, or if it's one of those complicated ones where I have to dig in and check a bunch of dense policy language to see what's actually covered... I just, I can't even bring myself to open it. I’ll look at it and my brain just sort of goes, "Nope, not right now, we can't handle that." 

So I’ll tell myself, "Okay, I'll just knock out the easy ones first to build some momentum." And then I’ll just spend hours doing all these really easy, quick tasks—like simple address updates or basic approvals that just take two clicks. I'll just keep putting off the hard ones, bypassing them in the queue, telling myself I'll get to them after lunch, or after my next break, until suddenly it's 4:30 and I'm basically out of time for the day. And then those complicated files just sit there, and I have to roll them over to the next day, which really messes up my turnaround time metrics. It's like the second I realize a task is going to take actual, heavy brainpower and I really have to think, I just find any excuse to avoid it and do the easy stuff instead.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself easily distracted by noises, activity around you, or unrelated thoughts when you are trying to work?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It's... it's honestly one of the biggest reasons I struggle with those complicated claims files I mentioned earlier. Our office setup is this open-plan thing, which I guess was supposed to foster collaboration or whatever, but for me, it's just a nightmare of distractions. 

Like, if I'm trying to read through a really dense medical history report—one of those ones where you have to cross-reference dates of service with the specific billing codes to make sure they aren't double-dipping—and the people in the pod next to me start talking about a claim they're working on, it's game over. Even if it's work-related, even if they're just discussing a routine dental pre-auth, my brain just completely abandons what I'm doing and latches onto their conversation. I'll be sitting there staring at my screen, but I'm actually listening to them debate whether a root canal was medically necessary. 

And it's not just other people, either. It's my own brain. I'll be right in the middle of a sentence in a policy document, and suddenly I'll remember, like, "Oh, I need to pick up dry cleaning," or "Did I ever reply to my mom's text about Sunday dinner?" or even just some random trivia fact I read on Reddit three days ago. And once that unrelated thought pops in, my attention just completely slides right off what I'm reading. 

It's so frustrating because I'll realize I've been staring at the same paragraph for five minutes, and I have no idea what it says. I end up having to reread the exact same section three, four, maybe five times before the information actually sticks and I can process what it means for the claim. It's like my focus is covered in Teflon or something, nothing sticks to it if there's even the slightest bit of noise or a random thought passing through my head. So yeah, distractibility is a huge, huge issue for me all day long.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly confirms being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like coworkers' conversations and by their own unrelated thoughts.

So, yeah, "driven by a motor" doesn't really sound like me. I'm probably more of a stalling engine, if anything. Just really sluggish when it comes to getting moving on things, rather than always being on the go.

Before I was 12? Um... yeah, actually. It's funny you ask that because looking back, this whole thing... it really wasn't brand new for me at all. I think it's just been going on for so long that I sort of accepted it as normal. 

Like, if you look at my old report cards from elementary school—my mom actually kept a bunch of them in this big plastic storage bin in her garage, which I ended up looking through when I helped her clean it out a couple years ago—there was definitely a massive pattern. Every single year, from like first grade all the way up, the teachers would write basically the exact same paragraph in the comments section. They’d always start off by saying I was a "bright" kid, or that I had a lot of potential, you know, probably just to soften the blow for my parents before getting to the bad stuff. 

But then the rest of the note was always about how I was just completely scattered. They’d write about how I constantly lost my worksheets. And it's true, I vividly remember my desk in, like, third and fourth grade being this absolute black hole of crumpled-up papers, old folders, and broken pencils. The teacher would hand out a math worksheet, and somehow between her handing it to me and the time we were supposed to turn it in, it would just vanish. I'd usually find it three weeks later stuffed at the very bottom of my backpack underneath a gym shirt. 

And they always noted that I missed verbal instructions, too. Like, the teacher would stand at the front of the room and explain step-by-step exactly how we were supposed to do a science project, and I'd be looking right at her, but my brain would be entirely focused on, like, a weird bug crawling on the window, or I'd be daydreaming about a video game. So then everyone else would start working, and I’d just be sitting there, having absolutely no clue what we were actually supposed to be doing. Because of that, the teachers constantly had to come over to my desk and give me these one-on-one reminders just to get me to finish my classwork. They'd have to literally tap on my desk and say, "Okay, focus back on the spelling test," or whatever it was we were doing. 

So, yeah... it’s definitely not a new thing that just started at this insurance job. It’s kind of always been there. I guess the stakes were just a lot lower back then when it was a spelling worksheet and not a claimant's health insurance file, you know? But the actual feeling of just completely losing track of what I'm supposed to be doing and losing my papers? Yeah, that’s been happening since I was a little kid.

Losing things? Yeah... yeah, that is a massive, massive daily struggle for me. It’s actually ridiculous how much time I spend every single day just... hunting for things I literally just had in my hands a second ago. It’s like my workspace has this invisible black hole on it. 

Take my headset, for example. I have to wear this wireless headset for the claimant calls, right? And sometimes I’ll take it off just for a second to rub my ears, or maybe I’ll stand up to stretch my legs while I’m reading a long, boring policy document on my monitor. I will set the headset down, and I swear to you, I don't even leave my cubicle, but when a call comes in two minutes later and the software starts beeping, I cannot find it. I’ll be tearing through my desk drawers, looking under my chair, lifting up stacks of paper in a total panic, and I’ll eventually find it resting on top of the filing cabinet behind me, and I have absolutely zero memory of turning around and putting it there. 

And it’s even worse with paperwork and notes. If the main database is lagging, which it does all the time, I’ll jot down a claimant’s callback number on a sticky note so I don't lose it. I’ll stick it right to the plastic edge of my monitor. Or at least, I think I do. But then I’ll go to actually make the call, and the sticky note is just gone. Did it fall? Did I accidentally throw it away with my lunch wrapper? I’ll spend twenty minutes moving every single object on my desk trying to find this one little yellow square of paper. Half the time I find it stuck to the bottom of my coffee mug, or stuck to the back of a completely unrelated printed claim form that I was reviewing. 

Speaking of claim forms, I lose those constantly, too. If I have to print out a physical faxed appeal to highlight the medical codes—because sometimes squinting at them on the screen gives me a headache—I will somehow manage to lose the physical paper between the communal printer and my desk. Or I'll set it down on my desk to answer a quick email, and then it's just buried under a mountain of other files, and I have to print the whole thing out all over again. 

And it’s not even just desk stuff, it’s my access badge to even get into the building. I’m supposed to keep it clipped to my belt on one of those retractable lanyards, but I’ll take it off to scan into the parking garage gate from my car window. I’ll toss it onto the passenger seat, completely forgetting that I need it to actually open the glass doors to the lobby. So I’ll get all the way up to the front doors, my coffee in one hand, my bag in the other, and realize I don't have my badge. I either have to do the walk of shame all the way back out to the parking garage, or I have to stand there awkwardly waiting for someone from the underwriting department to walk by and badge me in. They all know me by now, too, which is just embarrassing. It’s just... I’m constantly, constantly searching for the basic tools I need to just exist and do my job. It’s exhausting, honestly.
